This is a hoary bat call that was detected at the Los Angeles Zoo using a bat echolocation monitoring device. Hoary bats are a migratory bat species that travel from Canada to south America every fall.  They only roost in foliage so they are sensitive to urbanization and are great indicators of ecosystem health.  The long term monitoring device is in place to collect long term data on Los Angeles bats and to educate zoo visitors and the public about local bats and the important roles they play in ecosystems. The project is a collaboration between the Los Angeles Zoo and the United States Forest Service.  All species are identified by using Sonobat bat call analysis software.

Mexican free-tailed bats are one of the most common and urban-adapted bat species in Los Angeles and other areas around the southwest.  In fact, they roost in the Tree Top Terrace at the L.A. Zoo.  The L.A. Zoo occasionally offers twilight tours to the public so they can view this species emerge from the roost to hunt for insects. I went on a bug run earlier today and when I walked out of the store with my full cricket container I heard a woman screaming just up the street. I thought that maybe she had a snake or something so I walked over there with my cricket container in hand. I got there and she's hollering "It's a bat! Kill it! Kill it!" I said "There's no need for that." I look down and see a small brown bat on the sidewalk that as far as I could tell was unharmed. I explained that bats are voracious mosquito eaters and a benefit to have around. She calmed down and asked me why it wasn't flying. I told her that bats can't take off from the ground. I was able to get the bat to grab hold of my cricket container. One of the better ideas I've had in a while. So I never touched it or came close to getting bit. The big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus) is a widespread species of bat found throughout North America, Central America, the Caribbean, and extreme northern South America.

description: This Southeastern Myotis was caught in a harp trap in the Ordway-Swisher Biological Field Station in Florida, where it was leaving its roost to hunt. It can be identified by the hairs on its toes and how the wing attaches at the bat's ankle. It is obviously in the Order Chiroptera due to its furry wings.

Most of the reason I (originally) picked this species in particular as the identification for this particular bat is that it is listed as one of the species that is known to live at the UF bat houses. They all flew by too quickly for me to get a really good look. However, I can say for certain that the ones I saw were microchirpterans (small bats), in Order Chiroptera (of which all bats are members). These mammals are characterized by their membranous wings and fur, as opposed to the feathers of birds.

When we were doing the mothing night at Parr Park @kimberlietx found one there. I didn't really get great pictures of that one so I left it out but still I see why the data on dead things is so viable so I am kind of singing a different tune about not getting dead things; from now on I am adding them to my page. description: Order: Chiroptera. Easily identified by being the only true volant species of mammals and having wings comprised of a thin membrane of skin called a patagium that stretches across the last 4 elongated phalanges. The thumb is free and bears a claw. The have a robust pectoral girdle, large clavicle and a feeled sternum for flight. This flock was observed leaving the bat houses en masse on UF's campus to forage at dusk. Other features of this order that could not directly be observed include females having thoracic or pectoral teats, the ulna is reduced while the radius is elongated, and the acetabulum opens dorsally rather than ventrally (like most mammals) to allow for hanging up-side-down. Observed in cool (upper  50s F), dry conditions. The species is known via signage at the bat houses.

description:
This little girl I had to pick up from a bar because someone stepped on her wing. I didn’t want to post this until I knew her fate, but it’s safe to say now. It was almost freezing and midnight when I picked her up, and the only reason I was given the opportunity is because my ex-boss grad student called me, we both worked with bats. I was the closest and had already been to Bat World once that week so... 
I basically kept her warm and offered her water until the morning, where I prayed that I wouldn’t wake up to a dead bat. Fortunately, she made it, was taken to BWS early that morning and given painkillers, antibiotics and fluids. She is having her wing amputated and will never have to search for food again. She will have a whole colony of handicapped bats to socialize and cuddle with. I honestly feel if given the choice, bats will not miss flying. Most of flying for them is a huge energy drain, and not exactly something they do for fun. As highly social creatures, I don’t think she’ll miss it at all as long as she has a colony and is hand-fed. Please consider a small donation to BWS as Tadarida brasiliensis can live up to 15 years, and she’ll use up a lot of resources in her life. https://batworld.org/ways-to-donate/

I parked after exiting and thought about slipping back up the exit ramp on foot with my phone to take a better pic, but ominous, I had no idea there would be so many exiting cars this time of night! I don’t know how the little guy/gal could possibly be handling all the commotion! It’s a warmish, humid day, so I don’t think he was trying to escape the cold. But maybe the wind? Maybe the bright light attracts bugs? But it’s still pretty early in the year for bugs, especially downtown, I would think.

description: I was excited to have a chance to record this bat. There has been building high pressure for days with windy afternoons and bat activity has notably decreased. I am not clear if it is migration or weather. After trying for around 20 minutes with no passes (Tadarida brasilliensis and Parastrellus hesperus have been easy to record until recently) I walked back to the pool. There was a lone large bat at the pool that I originally thought was a Lesser Nighthawk but it seemed a little small for a LENI and it loudly slapped the water each time it drank. Lesser Nighthawks do not really drink that way. It seemed different/larger more “there” than the TADBRA, and I haven’t really seen the TADBRA at the pool like this. I was not surprised to see it identified as a different species, it sounded different via the sound conversion software as soon as I played it back. I have been using Joe Szewczak’s Echolocation Call Characteristics of California Bats and while I am just learning as far as I can tell this sonogram appears to match LASXAN. Recorded with iPhone XS Max and Echo Meter Touch 2 Pro ultrasonic module, the associated EMT bat detector app uses Kaleidoscope identification technology. I compressed the x-axis for the default screen shot in order to show more of the duration. Recorded as the bat repeatedly approached for drinks of water at last light.

Eastern Red Bat
•	Trophic level: Secondary consumer
•	Description: A common bat in the area, with orange-red fur and a tiny, scrunched-looking face. A few other bat species live in the area but differ in color (Silver-haired Bat) as well as size (Tricolored Bat). Most migrate south in the fall, so to find one at this time of year is a little surprising. 
•	Life Cycle: Breeding starts in autumn, and pups are born in the summer. Females can have up to five pups in a litter, which is unusual for bats. Migrate to the southeastern US and northern Mexico for the winter.
•	Stage: Based on appearance and time of year, and adult. 
•	Sex: Would be VERY difficult to get a good look, although females are more brown and gray in color. Too tough to say based on the light in the photos. 
•	Habitat: Widely distributed throughout the eastern half of the continental US, often near forest edges and in coastal areas. This one was seen chasing bugs over a pond at a forest edge.
•	Predator: American Crows could eat bats hiding in leaf piles. 
•	Prey: Flying insects like the Eastern Saltmarsh Mosquito

a) These Mexican Free-tailed Bats belong in the Molossidae family within the order Chiroptera. The Chiroptera order contains all bat species, which are the only mammalian species capable of true powered flight, with heavily modified forelimbs that have long phalanges connected by skin membranes. The Molossidae family contains free-tailed bat species.
b) These bats were observed on 11/14/2021, with clear weather that slowly cooled in temperature as the sunset progressed. The temperature reached a low of about 55°, after I had observed the bats for just over 30 minutes.
c/d) These bats were observed flying out from the bat houses at Lake Alice in a constant stream as they departed their home to hunt for food. They started their flight at sunset, passing above the heads of human onlookers, even within several feet. A red-shouldered hawk also attempted to catch the bats before (and while) they left the bat houses by swooping talons-first under the houses several times, but failed to catch any prey as far I am aware.

description:
This bat was roosting alone in a crevice that was only 1 cm wide. It was captured under a VDWR scientific collecting permit and USDA Forest Service research permit. The bat was a 4.9g adult male, FA of 30mm, first captured and banded in 2018 within a few meters of where we found it this time. The bat was an adult when first captured and had an identical weight and forearm measurement. 

Upon recapturing the bat we discovered it had a recent compound fracture to its femur, so we brought it to a wildlife rehabilitation center for evaluation and treatment. It's unclear how it got the injury. This site is frequented by a lot of people - it's possible that someone stepped on whatever rock the bat was roosting under.

Update on 26 June 2022: The bat survived surgery and is in recovery. It has limited use of its injured leg (portion of femur missing), but gets around relatively well. Radiographs show some trauma to its pelvis that the vet did not notice at first, so they will keep him for a bit longer to assess his chances of being released. I've added a recent photo taken by the wildlife rehabber (photo 4).

Update on 14 September: The bat spent the summer being rehabilitated. He's able to fly, forage, and groom himself despite not being able to use the leg, and he now weighs 5.7g, therefore was deemed ready for release. I'm very happy to report that today I took him back to the capture site and released him (photos 5 and 6).

SonoBat states that "[t]he notion behind the Standard View feature is to allow call pulses to be viewed at a fixed time scale so the user always views calls of certain durations at a similar scale. This aids in developing the “sight picture” or “gestalt” for the appearance of different call types from different species, supporting qualitative recognition."  For this observation, the duration is set at Sonobat's standard 10ms.

The number to the right of the species name at the top of the second spectrogram screenshot is the species or "call decision" score, which Sonobat defines as "a measure of how closely the current parameter set approaches the multidimensional space of a known parameter set.  A value above .50 indicates a likely result."

High frequency recording made with Echo Meter Touch 2 Pro microphone connected to old Fire tablet on the beach.

I had a blacklight running about 5 meters away at the edge of the beach and dunes to attract and document insects and ran my echo meter microphone for a minute around 19:43 and then something went wrong. I fixed it around 20:38 and it ran until 22:30. On the longer session it was triggered almost 200 times, all by Tadarida brasiliensis. I uploaded three observations from this night, assuming there were plenty of Tadarida in the area but no other species detected.

I set the echo meter up the following night as well, a little deeper in past the dunes and recorded another species or two with higher frequency calls.

Check out the Bat Spectrogram project here: https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/bat-spectrograms

More info about how to view spectrograms on Kaleidoscope (free software by Wildlife Acoustics) here: https://youtu.be/1AgxZh_mfOc

High frequency recording made with Echo Meter Touch 2 Pro microphone connected to old Fire tablet in past the dunes. 

I had blacklights running with a sheet about 5 meters away to attract and document insects and ran my echo meter microphone from 18:12-19:52 then something went wrong. I fixed it and ran it again from 21:56-22:12. The mic was triggered over 400 times, mostly by Tadarida brasiliensis but also two or three other species with higher frequency calls. 

I set the echo meter up the night prior, right on the beach near a blacklight and only recorded Tadarida brasiliensis.

description: Pictures I took of the famous Mexican Free-tailed Bat colony under the Congress Avenue bridge in Austin, TX.

We occasionally encounter interesting wildlife *indoors* as well! Generally the best thing to do if a Bat finds its way inside is to simply open a door or window and allow it to leave. It doesn't take them long to find their way out usually. In this case however, circumstances required that I assist this one. I have a lot of experience legally handling bats in the past however, and was safely able to render emergency help to this amazing creature. 

I'm not sure how he found his way in to visit us (in an old farmhouse with open chimneys), but this guy calmly toured the house for a while it seems. I thought I saw something out of the corner of my eye a few times. It wasn't until a couple hours later, near 2:00 A.M., that I more clearly saw him flying around upstairs. I was able to confine him to one room, in which he flew really slowly (for a Bat) and calmly, investigating the surroundings, and me. He flew directly to within a few inches of my face, and then tightly around me, clearly scanning me with ultrasound a couple times. They are so silent at audible frequencies at such times, but I could hear or maybe feel the low frequency waves of air that the wings were making. That is hard to describe, but I have been around many thousands of Bats at extremely close quarters, and am intrigued how they seem to massage the air as they fly. This one was flying with absolute minimum forward velocity, and was beautiful to watch as it circled and investigated the room. 

It was ultimately necessary that I gently envelope him in a towel and actually take him outside, which I accomplished with as little stress to him as possible. I have a lot of experience in a technique that I learned years ago in Florida. I really think that Bats, being as incredibly intelligent as they are, calm down when they realize they are not being threatened or hurt, only gently swaddled in a soft cloth as it were. This one, in any case, stopped struggling and making audible sounds quite quickly, after I positioned him to be able to see well, and scan me with ultrasound through his mouth. By the time I had shown him to my Mother who had woken up, and I had taken a couple photos with a wooden ruler for scale, he was calmly resting in my loose grip, even with his mouth closed. When I took him outside, he raised up on his forearms, looked all around, and took off - not madly away, but closely circled me again 360 degrees, and then off in the direction of our old barn, where I suspect he roosts during the day. I often see multiple large Bats emerge from a high window of that barn. 

It wasn't easy to make photographs of him without another pair of hands, but I managed these few closeups by myself. I would have liked a better view of one forearm along the ruler (a standard useful measurement of Bats), of the ears and nose features, and of genitalia (which were visible and male), but I needed both hands to position him, with no good way to operate a camera at the same time, and didn't want to risk any more stress to him than was necessary to release him safely outside, so am happy I got any pictures at all actually. Forearm length from the photo I got I would estimate to be around 44-45 millimeters. I did not see any visible external parasites as I have sometimes found on wild Bats, but did not take the time to really examine for them in this case. 

Also, that photo in flight was a surprise - that it would show much of anything at all with a camera-phone, without a strobe flash. 

My Mother, who turns 100 years old the day that I am posting this observation, tells the story of rescuing an apparently orphaned young Bat off the pavement in front of her house when she was young in Fort Myers, Florida, in the 1930's. I, of course, don't know if it was really a "baby" bat, or just an adult that ended up on the ground, but she says it would spend the day roosting under the collar of her dress or blouse. Be that as it may, I enjoyed being able to show her *this* particular beautiful Bat, and I saved this observation until today, her 100th Birthday, in her honor. Mom says, "I have always liked Bats."

This juvenile female Lasionycteris noctivagans was recovered by a San Diego Humane Society Animal Control Officer after discovered in a residential area west of Otay Lakes.  This is a very rare migratory bat for our area.  Only four have previously been physically observed and recorded in San Diego County, most recently in 1985.  It was assessed as healthy and nourished by Cindy and Chris, two volunteer bat rehabilitators affiliated with San Diego Humane Society Project Wildlife.  Following test flights in a flight cage, the bat was transported and safely released in a rural area east the original recovery site on the evening of 15 October.

The first five photos were taken indoors in a flight cage while the bat was being cared for.  The sixth image is of a bat fly posted separately to iNaturalist.  The seventh and eighth images show its echolocation call sonogram rendered in SonoBat shortly after release as it circled our position before departing.  The ninth image is a rendering of one of the Hoary bat's echolocation call sequences five minutes prior to the LANO release.

This beautiful female Western small-footed bat was rescued n early September.  It was brought into San Diego Humane Society Project Wildlife where an assessment found it was healthy.  Project Wildlife volunteer team members cared for her to ensure she was well nourished and hydrated and able to fly well (in a fight cage).  A diminutive species similar in size to a Myotis californicus, she weighed 4.9 grams at intake and 6.3 grams at release.
After passing all tests, she was transported back to Project Wildlife’s main campus in San Diego on 14 September for transport to a release site in the same general area as originally found.  Volunteer Vryce and I met and found a suitable habitat in the background of a friend of mine who resides less than a mile north of recovery coordinates.
As per my standard practice, I set up an ultrasonic acoustic detector proximate in advance of release.  Almost immediately another Western small-footed bat flew in and did a circle around me and my microphone, and stayed in the vicinity.  A couple of minutes later fellow volunteer Vryce opened the transport carrier, the rehab transporter was opened, and the female gently removed and held out on Vryce's palm.  She took off without hesitation.
The sonogram was recorded concurrently with release from Vryce’s hand.  It shows a conventional MYCI sequence and what looks like a quick succession of social calls at half the normal MYCI frequency.  The first screenshot (Image 6) is a compressed view.  The second (image 7) is an uncompressed view that shows there was a series of acoustic pulses that when expanded show each was a series of very short duration, short interval calls.  The sequence was also viewed in SonoBat (image 8).
It seems likely one of the two Western small-footed bats was communicating with the other.  It isn’t possible to tell which one made the social call.  Although purely speculative, it is fun to think the resident bat was a welcoming back party.

SPECIES: Evening Bat, Nycticeius humeralis Rafinesque, 1818
DISTINGUISHING: Small bat with brown body fur, black ears, and no fur on muzzle.
COLLECTION: EHW was carrying 2-day fallen dead palm fronds when he felt something trying to bite him.  Having been bitten by almost everything on the land and in the sea, he recognized the attempt.  He threw down the fronds and took a collection plastic bag from his pocket, found,  captured, and photographed a bat.  The specimen was held until dark to keep the released bat from day-time predation.  It was placed in a bush at a 2 m elevation adjacent to the capture locality.  All bats in Florida are protected. 
DATE, TIME: 12 October 2023, 3:14 PM
LOCALITY: 920 St. Andrews, Naples, Florida 34113
LONGITUDE, LATITUDE: 26.10716, 81.71515
DISTRIBUTION: Eastern and Midwest USA, NE Mexico.  Has recently spread further north, either replacing other species killed by White-nose Disease, or due to Global Warming.  Common in Florida except in the Keys.
ROOSTING: This species roosts in groups of a few to 100 specimens.  Sometimes other species are included in a roost.  Our specimen was in a dead palm frown on the ground.  It cannot take off in flight from the ground.  Why it remained 2 days on the ground is unclear.  It did not appear to be injured. 
SIMILAR SPECIES: Resemble Big Brown Bats, Eptesicus fuscus (Beauvois, 1796), but are much smaller.  And also uncommon in south Florida.
DANGEROUS: Bats have an undeserved reputation for frequently infecting humans with rabies.  This very rarely occurs.  Our rabid Racoon (Williams and Bunkley-Williams, 2019) was far more dangerous.
IMPORANTANCE: Unusual roosting and remaining on ground.

description:
Found March 19, 2022. Photos are over the course of 10 days.

Tiny little brown bat found wet and clinging to the side of a building. I kept him safe and sheltered. I named him Allspice. On the 10th day, he was brought inside (right before a cold snap), warmed, and turned over to a local rescue. They cared for him with several other bats of his kind and released them when the weather was warmer and a stable temperature. 

This little bat is a trooper and thrived amongst tough conditions. 

I'd like to learn the species.   

Photos: 
1 - Day one, found cold and wet. I sheltered him in place blocking wind and rain. 
2 - Attempt to photograph his face. 
3 - After a couple of days, he crawled between the screen door and outer door for warmth and remained for several days. At one point, I put a cloth over him to keep him warm. 
4 - Another view 
5 - Eventually tried to feed mealworms from the pet store (with tongs). They didn't have anything smaller. He was too tired to eat. He was taken to rescue the following morning after spending the night inside warming up.

description: HISTORIC PHOTOS.

Eastern red bats are widespread across eastern North America. 

The eastern red bat has distinctive fur, with males being brick red and females being a slightly more frosted shade of red.Both male and female eastern red bats have distinctive shoulder patches of white fur.

Eastern red bat breeding season starts in the autumn, and multiple males can sire a single litter. Pups are born in the summer, usually sometime between May and July. 

Eastern red bats are often attacked and killed by hawks and owls, or aggressive species like blue jays and crows. Eastern red bats are also killed by flying into cars, tall human-made structures, or wind turbines. 

The eastern red bat is evaluated as least concern by the IUCN, the lowest-priority conservation category. It has a wide geographic range, large population size, it occurs in protected areas, it tolerates some habitat disturbance, and its population size is unlikely to be declining rapidly.

Eastern red bats and other migratory tree bats are vulnerable to death by wind turbines via barotrauma. The eastern red bat has the second-greatest mortality from wind turbines, with hoary bats most affected.

While eastern red bats have been documented carrying the spores of the fungus that causes white-nose syndrome, no individuals have been observed with clinical symptoms (objective signs) of the disease.
